summary: This standards-track document defines a framework in which application logic and media processing run on different machines. A controlling application uses SIP to set up a control channel to a media server and then sends commands over it. Packages then define specific functions.

plainLanguage.summary: A director in one room tells a stage crew in another room what to play. This defines the phone line between them and how commands are sent.

subtitle: How an application server uses SIP to open a TCP control channel to a media server and then sends it commands.

tldr.problem: Real-time applications often run their logic on one server and their media processing on another, and need a standard way for the first to command the second without a second signaling protocol.
tldr.mechanism: A Control Client sends a SIP INVITE with SDP to set up a TCP (or TCP/TLS) Control Channel to a Control Server, then exchanges CFW messages (SYNC, CONTROL, REPORT, K-ALIVE) whose commands are defined by separate Control Packages.
tldr.outcome: The framework supplies the channel, correlation, keep-alive and long-running transaction handling, and leaves the actual commands to packages. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 6230 is a Proposed Standard from May 2011. It has not been obsoleted and no later RFC is listed as updating it.

sections.title: Why a Media Control Channel
sections.content:
Real-time media applications are often built with the application logic on application servers and the media processing on external servers such as media servers. This RFC defines the framework and protocol between the two. It came from the requirements in RFC 5167 and the needs of a centralized conference system, though it is not limited to those.

The document does not define a particular SIP extension for direct control. Other documents, called Control Packages, extend the framework with the actual commands.

The authors argue against Megaco (RFC 5125) for SIP networks: it duplicates many functions SIP already provides, forcing developers to translate between two mechanisms. SIP ([RFC3261]) is used as the rendezvous mechanism to establish and maintain the control connections.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of learning two different languages, the program uses the phone-call system it already knows to set up the line, and then sends orders over that line.

sections.title: Roles and Overall Design
sections.content:
A Control Client requests processing; a Control Server performs it, for example a media server offering mixing, announcements, and tone detection. A Control Channel is a reliable connection between them. A Framework Transaction is one message answered by a response code, and there are no provisional responses. The Transaction-Timeout is 10 seconds.

The channel is negotiated with a SIP INVITE and an SDP offer/answer, using COMEDIA (RFC 4145) to set up the connection. SIP brings service location through proxies and B2BUAs, TLS security, connection maintenance and application independence. The RFC explains why plain TCP is not enough: the SIP URI used for session setup must resolve to the same node that does session control, which SIP routing, with the server initiating the TCP connection back, ensures.

A client may request several Control Channels, each with its own INVITE dialog, for redundancy and load. The channels are orthogonal to any media session; media is attached later, for example through third party call control (RFC 3725), where a Control Client acts as a B2BUA between a User Agent and the Control Server.
sections.plainLanguage: One side asks for work and the other does it. They first agree on a private line using the normal calling system, and each line lasts as long as the call does.

sections.title: Setting Up the Control Channel
sections.content:
The client sends an INVITE whose SDP contains one Control Channel media line: m=application <port> TCP cfw, with TCP or TCP/TLS as the protocol. Implementations MUST support TCP and MUST support TLS, although using TLS in a given deployment is optional. SDP SHOULD use the default port, TCP 7563, unless local policy prohibits it, which lets administrators manage firewall policy.

COMEDIA attributes such as a=setup:active and a=connection:new decide who connects. It is RECOMMENDED that the controlling UAC initiate the connection, but a server MAY do so if topology prevents it. Each side MUST include a unique cfw-id SDP attribute, which must differ between offer and answer and stay constant for the life of the INVITE dialog usage. Using a=connection:existing reuses the connection and new re-establishes a failed one.

The channel and the dialog are linked: ending the SIP dialog, for example with BYE, ends the channel. A rejected offer (for example 488) or an m= line with port 0 means the server does not support or accept the channel.
sections.plainLanguage: The caller says on the phone, 'let us connect a private line, my ID is this.' The listener answers with its own ID. When the call ends, the line goes away too.

sections.title: Messages, Methods and Response Codes
sections.content:
Each framework message starts with the token CFW, a transaction identifier and then either a method (requests) or a status code (responses). Four methods exist and MUST be supported: SYNC, CONTROL, REPORT and K-ALIVE. Headers include Control-Package, Dialog-ID, Packages, Supported, Keep-Alive, Seq, Status, Timeout, Content-Type and Content-Length. The transaction identifier must be unique between a given client and server, and a client waits at least 2*Transaction-Timeout for a response.

The response codes cover only the framework transaction, not the success of a command inside a package. Examples are 200 (success), 202 (more to come through REPORT), 400 (bad syntax), 403 (refused by policy), 406 (out of sequence), 420 to 423 (package and transaction conflicts), 481 (no such dialog or transaction) and 500 (not understood).
sections.plainLanguage: Every note starts with the same secret word, then an ID number, then what you want. Replies carry the same ID so you know which question they answer.

sections.title: SYNC, CONTROL, REPORT and K-ALIVE
sections.content:
SYNC. Right after the connection opens, the active side sends a SYNC carrying a Dialog-ID equal to its own cfw-id. This ties the channel to its SIP dialog. A 481 means the dialog does not exist, and timeouts or errors end the channel and the dialog with a BYE. The initial SYNC also negotiates the Keep-Alive value, which SHOULD be 95 to 120 seconds and MUST NOT exceed 600 seconds, and a Packages list. If there are no common packages, the server answers 422 with a Supported header.

CONTROL. Carries a package command in its body. The server answers 200 when finished in time, or 202 with a Timeout header if the work will take longer than the Transaction-Timeout.

REPORT. After a 202, the server sends REPORTs with the same transaction ID. They start at Seq: 1, each adds 1, and a gap is answered with 406. Status: update refreshes the timer; Status: terminate ends it. The RFC recommends a Timeout between 10 and 15 seconds and refreshing at about 80% of it.

K-ALIVE. Keeps the channel alive through firewalls and NATs. The active side sends it, recommended after 80% of the keep-alive timer, and the passive side answers 200. If keep-alives fail, the dialog is torn down.
sections.plainLanguage: SYNC is saying hello and agreeing the rules. CONTROL is giving an order. If the job is slow, the crew sends progress notes (REPORT). K-ALIVE is saying 'still here' every so often.

sections.title: Control Packages and Extensibility
sections.content:
Packages specify the commands carried in CONTROL and REPORT bodies. They MUST NOT weaken the MUST and SHOULD statements of the framework but MAY strengthen weaker words. Each package must provide a name token, the message usage and directions, the CONTROL and REPORT body definitions, and a SHOULD-level audit section, and examples are strongly RECOMMENDED. An optional common XML schema in the appendix lets packages refer to a media dialog connection or a multiparty conference.

The framework itself is only minimally extensible. New methods, headers and status codes can come from Standards-Track RFCs. There is no version number and no negotiation mechanism. Unknown header fields MUST be ignored and an unknown method MUST get a 500 response.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework is the phone line and the rules for talking. The actual vocabulary of orders comes in separate booklets called packages.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The framework aims at confidentiality, integrity and assurance that the connected host is the intended one. Because the cfw-id travels across the SIP network, SIP clients MUST use appropriate security such as TLS and S/MIME in open networks.

Plain TCP is weak: anyone can see the data. Clients and servers MUST support TLS and SHOULD use it by default unless another protection is used or a protected environment is guaranteed. A TLS cipher suite of TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA MUST be supported. A TLS server MUST ask for a client certificate, allowing mutual authentication.

Policy, such as which channel may issue commands for which package or conference, can be tied to authentication. A command that is not permitted gets a 403, which carries no detail about the failure.
sections.plainLanguage: Without a lock, anyone can listen in on the line. So the line should be locked, and both sides should show ID, so only the right people can give orders.

messages.label: SIP 200 OK
messages.note: SDP answer with its own cfw-id.

messages.label: SIP BYE
messages.note: Ends the dialog and the channel.

items.label: Accepted
items.desc: Completed; more information will come through REPORT.

items.label: Forbidden
items.desc: Understood but refused; do not repeat.

items.label: Package not valid
items.desc: Target package not valid for this session.

items.label: No re-negotiation
items.desc: Recipient does not want to re-negotiate packages now.

items.label: No common package
items.desc: No package in the SYNC is supported.

items.label: Duplicate transaction
items.desc: An existing transaction has the same ID.

items.label: No such transaction
items.desc: For SYNC, the SIP dialog does not exist.

items.label: Not understood
items.desc: Recipient does not understand the request.
